web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Grading Room — Five Revenue Engines
question: What exactly does IGIL sell across loose stones, studded jewelry, colored gemstones, and education, and how does each segment work in the real world?

epigraph.quote: A diamond certificate does not create value out of thin air; it converts asymmetric information into liquid trust.
epigraph.author: Gemological Trade Principle

web_blocks.title: Revenue mix and the lab-grown diamond engine

web_blocks.html: IGIL generates roughly 97% of its revenue from certification and accreditation services. The remaining ~3% comes from gemological education and allied services [6]. Within certification, the mix has shifted decisively toward laboratory-grown diamonds (LGDs). Loose LGD certification accounts for roughly 54% of total certification revenue, while loose natural diamonds represent about 14% [11]. Studded jewelry (both natural and lab-grown) and colored gemstones supply the balance [11]. In Q2 FY27 (ended September 30, 2026), certification revenue rose 32% YoY to ₹387.5 Cr (₹3,875 million) out of ₹398.0 Cr total operating revenue. LGD categories drove roughly 73% of that incremental YoY growth [4, 11].

web_blocks.caption: IGIL Operating Segments, Mix & Recent Growth Trajectory (15M FY26 & Q2 FY27)
web_blocks.takeaway: LGD loose stones and LGD studded jewelry supply the vast majority of IGIL's growth, while AGL's colored-stone business adds a high-margin non-diamond leg.

web_blocks.title: Concrete end-to-end example 1: Loose lab-grown diamond certification in Surat

web_blocks.html: Consider a mid-sized CVD diamond grower in Surat that polishes 5,000 loose two-carat stones each month for US bridal wholesalers. Without third-party grading, a New York buyer cannot tell D-color from G-color or VVS2 from SI1 clarity. Nor can the buyer tell if the stone is CVD-grown rather than natural or treated with post-growth HPHT annealing. The grower therefore submits polished stone batches to IGI's Surat laboratory. Each stone passes through automated spectroscopic screening to confirm synthetic origin and detect treatments. Next, precision optical scanners measure proportions, and two independent gemologists grade the stone under controlled daylight-equivalent lighting.

Once graded, IGI laser-inscribes a microscopic report number onto the diamond's girdle. The mark is invisible to the naked eye but readable under a 10x loupe. IGI then issues a physical and digital QR-linked certificate detailing the 4Cs (Cut, Color, Clarity, Carat) and growth method [10]. The grower pays a fixed tiered fee per stone based on carat weight, not a percentage of wholesale price. That fee structure matters. Even as wholesale LGD prices fell sharply over 2023–2026, larger carat sizes (2-to-4 carats) pushed submissions into higher fee brackets. Meanwhile, lower retail prices drove certification volume up 37% YoY [4, 11].

web_blocks.title: Concrete end-to-end example 2: Studded jewelry certification for retail chains

web_blocks.html: Grading a finished engagement ring or tennis necklace is far harder than grading a loose stone. Prongs and metal settings hide facets and prevent direct weight measurement on a scale. An Indian national jewelry chain or US mall retailer launching a 10,000-piece lab-grown bridal collection sends finished jewelry batches to IGI's Mumbai or New York labs, or routes them through an IGI in-factory desk. Gemologists verify every mounted melee and center stone using non-destructive imaging. They also confirm metal purity hallmarks, estimate total carat weight from dimensional geometry, and issue a tamper-evident jewelry report.

For the retailer, that report solves two commercial problems at once. First, it reassures first-time LGD buyers who worry about paying diamond prices for cubic zirconia or moissanite. Second, it standardizes return and exchange policies across hundreds of stores. In Q2 FY27, LGD studded jewelry certification volume jumped 47% YoY. It is now IGIL's fastest-growing category as organized retail chains in India and North America scale LGD assortments [4, 5].

web_blocks.title: Concrete end-to-end example 3: Natural diamonds, colored gemstones (AGL), and gemology schools

web_blocks.html: In natural diamonds, a Surat exporter cutting 0.50-to-1.50 carat commercial bridal stones often picks IGI over GIA when speed and cost matter for mid-tier retail programs. That steady demand drove +8% YoY loose natural volume growth in Q2 FY27 [5]. In colored gemstones, value depends on geographical origin (such as Kashmir sapphire or Burmese ruby) and heat or oil treatments. IGIL's February 2026 purchase of AGL brought New York's premier origin-determination lab into the group [8, 9]. A dealer holding a $150,000 emerald submits it to AGL for spectroscopic trace-element fingerprinting. If AGL certifies Colombian origin with no clarity enhancement, the stone commands a substantial auction premium.

Finally, IGIL operates 21 Schools of Gemology globally [13]. Tuition contributes only a small share of revenue, but the schools serve as a strategic funnel. They train retail sales associates, designers, and independent jewelers in IGI's grading terminology. As a result, the next generation of counter staff instinctively asks for and trusts an IGI certificate.

web_blocks.text: Revenue Mix Evolution: Loose LGD, Studded Jewelry, Natural & Education

web_blocks.html: During the 15-month fiscal transition period ended March 31, 2026, IGIL generated ₹15,976M in revenue across 16.45 million reports. Growth accelerated in Q2 FY27 to ₹398.0 Cr revenue (+31% YoY) across 4.35 million reports (+26% YoY) [4][5]. The mix shift toward finished studded jewelry and high-volume lab-grown diamond (LGD) certification is unmistakable. In Q2 FY27, LGD studded jewelry certification surged +47% YoY and loose LGD rose +37% YoY. As US, European, and Indian jewelers launch LGD bridal and fashion lines, they increasingly demand finished-piece certificates instead of relying only on loose-stone dossiers [4][5].

In January and February 2026, IGIL acquired American Gemological Laboratories (AGL) for $13.2 million [8]. This deal opens a high-margin fourth pillar in prestige colored gemstones such as emeralds, rubies, and sapphires. Colored-stone grading requires scarce specialist skill in origin determination and treatment detection. Consequently, it commands much higher per-report ASPs than standard melee diamond screening.

Pricing across segments follows a structured rate card rather than ad-valorem percentages of stone value. Loose diamond reports are billed by carat-weight brackets (0.30–0.49 ct, 0.50–0.99 ct, 1.00–1.49 ct, and 1.50+ ct), while studded jewelry is billed per piece or per parcel tier [3]. This weight-and-piece model shields IGIL from direct pass-through of wholesale LGD price declines, though large-volume customers negotiate tiered annual rebates [3][4].

Geographically, India acts as the primary processing and export engine, handling most global LGD and studded jewelry cutting and setting. Meanwhile, Belgium (Antwerp), the US (New York and Los Angeles), Hong Kong, Dubai, and Bangkok capture high-value natural, trade-hub, and retail-facing certification demand [3][8].

On the retail side, omnichannel and direct-to-consumer (D2C) jewelry brands now embed QR-coded digital IGI dossiers directly on product pages. Online shoppers can thus verify diamond fluorescence, table percentage, and polish symmetry before checking out [28].

book_paragraphs: To understand why IGIL earns operating margins above 60%, walk through the problem a jewelry buyer faces at a retail counter. A two-carat diamond ring sits under warm halogen spotlights. To an ordinary shopper, a D-color flawless stone and an F-color slightly included stone look virtually identical, yet their fair values differ by thousands of dollars. Even more critically, a lab-grown diamond grown in a Surat vacuum chamber has the exact same crystal lattice, refractive index, and hardness as a natural diamond mined in Botswana. Only specialized spectroscopy and trained eyes can separate them.

IGIL monetizes that information gap across five distinct service lines. Roughly 97% of its revenue comes from certification fees, while about 3% comes from its 21 Schools of Gemology. Within certification, loose lab-grown diamonds represent the largest single pillar at roughly 54% of certification revenue, while loose natural diamonds contribute around 14%. Studded jewelry—both natural and lab-grown—along with a rapidly growing colored gemstone practice account for the remainder.

book_subsections.title: How Stones Move Through the Laboratory
paragraphs: Consider a typical week for a Surat CVD diamond manufacturer producing 5,000 polished stones for American bridal wholesalers. Rather than shipping stones across continents before knowing their grades, the manufacturer delivers sealed parcels to IGI's local laboratory. Automated screening machines first verify that no undeclared natural or simulant stones are mixed in. Next, optical scanners map facet angles and proportions, and two independent gemologists grade color and clarity against master stones. Finally, a precision laser inscribes a microscopic IGI report number onto the stone's girdle, and a QR-coded report is generated. The manufacturer pays a fixed tiered fee per report based on carat weight—not a percentage of the stone's selling price.

That fee-per-report model explains a seeming paradox in the diamond market. Between 2023 and 2026, wholesale prices of lab-grown diamonds fell precipitously as reactor capacity expanded. For diamond growers and retailers, falling prices squeezed margins. For IGIL, cheaper lab-grown diamonds meant consumers upgraded from one-carat stones to two- and three-carat stones, pushing submissions into higher carat-weight fee tiers while total unit volumes jumped 37% YoY in Q2 FY27.

Natural diamonds follow a steadier, mature cadence. Exporters cutting 0.50-to-1.50 carat commercial stones in Surat often use IGI for mid-tier retail programs where rapid turnaround matters as much as prestige, producing +8% YoY volume growth in loose natural diamonds during Q2 FY27 even while the broader natural diamond market remained sluggish.

book_subsections.title: Studded Jewelry, Colored Gemstones, and the Education Funnel
paragraphs: The same trust dynamic plays out in finished jewelry. When an Indian jewelry chain or a US retailer launches a lab-grown bridal line, prongs and metal settings hide the stone's weight and lower pavilion. IGI's jewelry labs verify stone identity, estimate carat weight non-destructively, and issue a retail-ready certificate. For omnichannel retailers, that certificate reduces return disputes and reassures skeptical first-time buyers. In Q2 FY27, LGD studded jewelry volumes rose 47% YoY—the fastest growth rate across the company.

In February 2026, IGIL extended this trust model into high-value colored stones by acquiring American Gemological Laboratories in New York for $13.2 million. Colored stones depend heavily on country-of-origin and treatment disclosures—whether a sapphire is unheated Kashmir or heated Sri Lankan—and AGL's reputation gives IGIL an immediate gateway to high-ticket ruby, sapphire, and emerald dealers worldwide. Supporting all four grading lines are IGI's 21 gemology schools, which train retail staff and designers globally in IGI's grading language—quietly reinforcing brand preference at the point of sale.

book_subsections.title: Walkthrough of the Four Profit Engines
paragraphs: Let us walk inside an IGI laboratory so this business stops being an abstract line item and becomes tangible. Imagine a mid-sized Surat grower who has just pulled 5,000 carats of CVD lab-grown rough from his reactors, cut and polished them into 1-carat to 3-carat solitaires, and needs to ship them to a bridal wholesaler in Dallas. Without a third-party certificate, the Dallas buyer will only pay distressed bulk prices. So the exporter drops the parcel at IGI's Surat lab. Within days, each diamond is weighed to the thousandth of a carat, screened for strain and growth type, graded for color and clarity under standardized lighting, laser-inscribed on the girdle with a micro-serial number, and sealed in a tamper-evident dossier.

Now shift to the second engine: studded jewelry certification. Picture a major Indian retail chain preparing 40,000 diamond-studded rings and pendants for the Diwali wedding season. Grading loose melee stones before setting isn't enough—a stone can chip during setting, or an unscrupulous supplier might swap a high-color stone for a lower one. IGI tests the finished piece non-destructively, verifies diamond origin (natural vs. lab-grown) using spectroscopy, estimates total carat weight and color-clarity range, and issues a jewelry card that sits inside the velvet box at the retail counter. That single card transfers trust from a ₹2,000-crore retail brand straight to a nervous first-time buyer.

Finally, consider the education arm—21 gemological schools across global hubs. While education is a single-digit percentage of revenue, it acts as a self-funding talent pipeline and brand moat. Thousands of retail sales associates, jewelry designers, and rough sorters learn the 4Cs using IGI terminology, ensuring that when they become buyers or merchandisers, IGI is the language they naturally specify.

book_subsections.title: Why Rate-Card Pricing Matters More Than Stone Prices
paragraphs: One of the most frequent questions investors ask about IGIL is simple: if a 1-carat lab-grown diamond now wholesales for a fraction of what it cost three years ago, doesn't IGIL's revenue per stone collapse alongside it? The answer lies in how IGIL bills its customers. Unlike an auction house that charges a percentage of hammer price, IGIL charges a fixed fee schedule based on carat-weight brackets and report format.

Think about what that means for unit economics. Whether a 1.5-carat lab-grown oval solitaire wholesales for $400 or $180, the optical spectrometer scan, the inclusion plotting under 10x magnification, the color master-stone comparison, and the girdle laser inscription require the exact same gemologist minutes. While large volume exporters do negotiate tiered rebates as their annual parcel counts climb, IGIL's revenue per report is anchored to physical labor and lab capacity—not commodity diamond prices.

As jewelry retailers shift toward finished studded pieces—bracelets, tennis necklaces, and halo engagement rings—the certification unit shifts from a single loose stone to a finished piece blending gold, melee diamonds, and a center stone. In Q2 FY27, studded LGD jewelry certification grew 47% year-on-year, proving that retail adoption is expanding IGIL's addressable fee pool faster than loose-stone price deflation.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: THE JEWELRY COUNTER MOAT
callouts.text: When a US or Indian consumer buys a ₹1.5 lakh studded ring, a ₹1,200 certification card is less than 1% of the retail ticket—yet it closes the sale. That tiny cost-to-value ratio is why retailers rarely skimp on certification.

book_subsections.title: AGL and the Untapped Colored Gemstone Opportunity
paragraphs: While diamonds account for the bulk of IGIL's volume, the early 2026 acquisition of American Gemological Laboratories (AGL) for $13.2 million opens a qualitatively different profit pool: high-value colored stones. Unlike diamonds—where grading is standardized around the 4Cs—emeralds, rubies, and sapphires derive massive price premiums from geographic origin (such as Colombian emeralds or Burmese rubies) and whether the stone has been heat-treated or oiled.

A single prestige origin report from a recognized lab like AGL can command fees several times higher than a standard diamond dossier, because the buyer is paying for provenance verification on a five- or six-figure gem. By plugging AGL's prestige brand into IGI's 36-laboratory global distribution network across Mumbai, Bangkok, Antwerp, and Dubai, management has a low-capex lever to lift blended revenue per report over the next three to five years.

book_subsections.title: Digital Dossiers and the E-Commerce Trust Layer
paragraphs: Think about how a modern engaged couple shops for a diamond ring compared to their parents. Twenty years ago, a buyer walked into a local jeweler, looked through a loupe, and relied on the salesperson's pitch. Today, a buyer in Austin or Mumbai compares twenty lab-grown oval diamonds side by side on a smartphone screen—often buying a ₹1.5 lakh solitaire without ever holding it in hand before delivery.

That e-commerce shift is impossible without a standardized digital grading report. Every IGI certificate carries a scannable QR code and an online verification portal showing exact proportions, symmetry, fluorescence, and laser inscription numbers. As online and omnichannel penetration rises across both US bridal and Indian festive jewelry, IGI's digital dossier becomes the indispensable checkout trust layer.

book_callouts.title: What This Means for an Owner
book_callouts.text: IGIL prices per report by carat-weight tier rather than taking a cut of diamond value. That insulates its top line from falling wholesale LGD prices as long as lower retail prices stimulate higher unit volumes and larger carat sizes.
